blocks.text: The chapter is a defense of the missionaries’ conduct among the Thessalonians. Their bold proclamation is set beside repeated denials of error, deceit, flattery, greed, and the pursuit of human praise. Although Paul says they could have made a weighty claim as apostles, he instead emphasizes gentleness, affection, sharing both the good news and themselves, and exhortation directed toward a life worthy of God. The parental images describe care and encouragement within this account; they do not make authority a claim over others’ money, bodies, obedience, or lives.

The recollection of working “night and day” so as not to burden the congregation belongs to this defense of the missionaries’ motives. Other Pauline passages distinguish several economic relationships—such as gifts, wages, hospitality, partnership, collections, obligation, and labor—rather than presenting one universal arrangement. Here self-support is part of this team’s account of integrity, not a rule that makes unpaid ministry, overwork, or one funding practice mandatory in every setting.

In verses 13–16, the Thessalonians’ suffering is compared with that of assemblies in Judea, and the language about Jews is severe. The available accounts support a setting of real social pressure, but they do not identify one exhaustive persecuting group or establish a single cause such as formal state persecution. This caution matters when reading the chapter’s polemical language: it should not be expanded into collective blame.

There is a textual variant in verse 7: some readings say the missionaries were “gentle” among the Thessalonians, while another reads “infants,” immediately before the image of a nursing caregiver. The nursing-care comparison remains central to the sentence, but the wording just before it is uncertain.

The closing verses present separation as painful rather than indifferent: Paul says the team was absent in person but not in heart, repeatedly wished to return, and was hindered. Their hope, joy, and glory are tied to the Thessalonians’ future before the Lord. The passage shows strong attachment amid practical limits on travel without implying that every intended visit will take place.
